"The tonic syllable is generally the stressed syllable, though syllables are little differentiated by stress and in tone patterns 5 and 6 the syllable immediately after the tonic syllable, when it contains a long vowel, may be equally stressed with the tonic syllable." ... new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Tlingit has an empty rule. Story supplies the type (two lexical tones on the tonic syllable; stress weak and coincident with the tonic/stem syllable) and the domain (tone group, last word). Nothing in the catalog is contradicted since nothing was recorded.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tlingit (central dialect) has two lexical tones, high and low, contrastive only on the tonic syllable of the tone group (a unit of one or more grammatical words). Stress is weak ('syllables are little differentiated by stress') and falls on the tonic syllable, which is always a stem syllable and sits in the last word of the tone group; relative to the tone group it may be final, penultimate or antepenultimate (the latter two when suffixes/clitics follow the stem). So word stress is effectively root/stem-anchored and the tone-bearing syllable is the stressed one; it is not counted from an edge of the word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such. In tone patterns 5 and 6 (low-tone tonic on the penult or antepenult of the tone group) the syllable immediately after the tonic, if it has a long vowel, 'may be equally stressed with the tonic syllable' (p. 15). The precontour (pre-tonic syllables) is low-mid in pitch; its first syllable and closed/long-vowel syllables are slightly higher (p. 15).
new_statements.exceptions: Tone group extensions (syllabic clitics) are never tonic (p. 15-16). Laryngeals occur only as onsets of tonic syllables (p. 9, 13). Low tone does not occur with short vowels (p. 14). Story notes dialect differences in 'intonational features' (p. 2) and describes the central dialect only.
new_statements.identity_note: Story 1966 describes the central dialect of Tlingit (fieldwork 1959-1963 at Angoon, Admiralty Island, SE Alaska, with short visits to Hoonah, Juneau, Kake, Klukwan, Sitka, Carcross, Teslin); she notes dialects differ partly in 'intonational features' (p. 2). Buschmann 1857 treats 'die Sprache der Koloschen' (= Tlingit) from 18th-19th c. wordlists (Veniaminov's Sitka-area material, Lisiansky, Marchand/Chanal/Roblet, Wrangell, Davydov), not from fieldwork.

tone_statements.citation: Crippen, James A. 2019. The syntax in Tlingit verbs. Ph.D. dissertation, University of British Columbia. xxviii+925 pp. (DOI 10.14288/1.0388221; lingbuzz/005047.)
tone_statements.quote: Tone is phonologically significant, indicating lexical differences like low tone x̱aat /χàːt/ ‘root’ versus high tone x̱áat /χáːt/ ‘fish, salmon’ ... The Northern dialect of Tlingit has a tonal contrast between high (H) and low (L) tone that occurs on all vowels. ... the Southern Tlingit dialect has an additional falling contour tone represented as either /V̂ ː/ or /V́ V̀/ that occurs only on long vowels; there is no corresponding rising contour tone. The Tongass Tlingit dialect does not have phonemic tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 797, Appendix A 'Language background', sec. 2.2 'Vowels'; dialect split restated sec. 3 p. 799 with Table A.3
tone_statements.summary: Northern Tlingit: high vs low tone on all vowels; Southern adds a falling HL tone on long vowels; Tongass has no tone. Word stress on the stem/head noun; stressed short vowels high; tonal -H suffixes.

tone_statements.citation: Crippen, James A. 2015. Stem variation in Tlingit. Unpublished manuscript (incomplete draft, dated 2015-01-14). Alaska Native Language Archive item TL004C2015a.
tone_statements.quote: Tongass Tlingit is a dialect of Tlingit that lacks tone, instead having a distinction between plain and modified vowels. ... Open syllable invariable roots can only have long vowels, but the vowel may have either high or low tone. ... Closed syllable roots can have long or short vowels, and if long the vowel can have either high or low tone; short vowels can only have high tone. ... Closed verb roots with the -n stem appear with a short vowel, this vowel being obligatorily high tone in Northern Tlingit since the verb stem must be stressed.
tone_statements.locator: p. 11, sec. 2.1 (Tongass sentence); p. 13, sec. 2.3 'Invariable roots' (inventory sentences, Figure 2 on p. 14); p. 28, sec. 3.5 'Nasal stem -n' (stress sentence)
tone_statements.summary: Northern Tlingit vowels carry high or low tone (short root vowels only high); verb stems are obligatorily stressed, giving high tone on short stem vowels; the extinct Tongass dialect has laryngeal vowels and no tone.

tone_statements.citation: Crippen, James A. 2012-2013. Laryngeal vowels in Tongass Tlingit. Unpublished paper (University of British Columbia), with defence slides and proposal. Alaska Native Language Archive item TL004C2012a.
tone_statements.quote: It is one of the very few languages that contrast three different glottal states in its vowels, and unlike most others Tongass Tlingit is toneless. ... Tlingit dialects other than Tongass Tlingit are tonal and lack laryngeal vowels. The correspondences between the dialects are given in table 3. Leer (1991, 2001) has analyzed Tongass Tlingit’s vowel phonation inventory as the primary basis of tonogenesis in the other dialects, with stress accounting for some instances of Tongass /Vː/ as high tone but others as low tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 1, sect. 1 Introduction and p. 15, sect. 5 Discussion; Table 3 'Suprasegmental vowel correspondences between Tlingit dialects' on p. 16
tone_statements.summary: Tongass Tlingit is toneless, with plain, long, glottalized and fading vowels instead of tone; the other dialects are tonal (Table 3 marks high, low and falling tone on Sanya, Henya, Northern forms).

tone_statements.citation: Crippen, James A. 2010. Lingít Yoo X̱'atángi: A Grammar of the Tlingit Language (draft ms., 255 pp; Glottolog ref 409132).
tone_statements.quote: Tlingit dialects have various tone systems, with the majority form in Northern Tlingit having a two-way distinction between unmarked low tone and marked high tone, both of which are level. Southern Tlingit has a three- ... way tone system of low, high, and falling tones, with the falling tone having a contour that runs downward from the high tone to the low tone. Tongass Tlingit had a four-way nontonal system of syllable nuclei ... two-way tone system of Northern Tlingit may be evolving into a pitch accent system.
tone_statements.locator: §1.3.1 'Sounds' (Typological summary), pp. 9-10 (the '.. ' bridges a page break with footnotes); restated in §3.2.2.3 'Tone' with Table 3.3, pp. 49-50
tone_statements.summary: Northern Tlingit (majority form): two level tones, unmarked low vs marked high, maybe becoming pitch accent in nouns; Southern: high, low, falling; Transitional unclear; Tongass non-tonal register.

Proceedings of the Fifth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society (BLS 5), 461-463 [LSA/Crossref record and PDF: 461-470, because the file also contains J.-M. Hombert, 'Early Bantu Population Movements and Iron Metallurgy: The Linguistic Evidence', pp. 464-470]. doi:10.3765/bls.v5i0.2177. (Typescript, ca. 10 pp.: ANLA CA979Ha1979.)
tone_statements.quote: Tlingit, generally, distinguishes long and short vowels and has high and low toned syllables} but Tongass shows instead of tone distinctively different modified varieties of length. What is most striking and important (Krauss apud Pinnow 1976:19 and Leer 1978:5) is that while Tongass has a separate but simple pho-netic match for general Tlingit low tone, it has two non-predict-able kinds of length for general Tlingit high tone. ... Krauss has since reported (in press) that Leer now finds in the Heinyaa dialect two distinctive high tones corres-ponding to Tongass sustained and clipped
tone_statements.summary: General Tlingit has high- and low-toned syllables plus vowel length; the Tongass dialect has no tone but four vowel-length/laryngeal types instead; Heinyaa is reported to split high tone in two.

tone_statements.translation: The most interesting feature of Tongass Tlingit from a comparative point of view is that it differs from the rest of Tlingit in having a system of vowel nucleus modification which is basically non-tonal, but rather closely resembles that of Eyak. ... Following are the correspondences between the Tongass vowel nuclei and their tonal reflexes in the Saanyaa dialect of Saxman-Ketchikan and the Heinyaa dialect of Klawock-Craig, as well as with the Northern dialects, which include all other Tlingits. (V = short vowel, VV = long vowel; tones are high ´, falling ^, low `; low tone is left unmarked in the practical orthography of Northern Tlingit, since there are only 2 tones.)

tone_statements.summary: Tongass Tlingit is basically non-tonal (short, sustained, clipped, fading vowel nuclei), matching high, falling, low tones in Saanyaa-Heinyaa and the 2 tones (high, low) of Northern Tlingit.

tone_statements.citation: De Wolf, Gaelan. 1977. Tlingit phonology in a generative framework: an examination of phonological processes and abstract representation. M.A. thesis, University of British Columbia. (cIRcle retrospective digitization 2010, DOI 10.14288/1.0094182.)
tone_statements.quote: Tone in Tlingit is phonemic, and is marked on stem vowels which have a high or low tone, thus furnishing a total of sixteen distinctive syllables. According to Velten (1939: 66): Tlingit syllables may have high, low, or indifferent pitch. The difference between high and low tone may have a semantic value ... The distinction between low and indifferent pitch, however, is less essential. Stress, though generally associated with high tone, is not phonemic. ... Minimal pairs indicate the contrastive differences in high and low tones. High tone is marked by acute accent, low by grave accent.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 54-56, section II.8 'Tone' (first four sentences p. 54, 'phonemic.' tops p. 55, 'Minimal pairs.. grave accent.' p. 56)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Phonemic high vs low tone on stem vowels, from Boas, Velten and Naish/Story data; toneless suffixes take the tone opposite the stem; stress goes with high tone, not phonemic; Tongass has no tone.

tone_statements.quote: 3.1 Monosyllabic forms. When monosyllabic forms are substituted in frames it is apparent that the pitch contrasts represent two and only two tone levels. ... Two tone-stress phonemic units (henceforward called a tone unit) are postulated: high /´/ and low /`/, in which the tone is primary and the stress secondary. The pitch levels of the unstressed syllables are none phonemic.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: the Boas 1917 pp. 11-12 passage and both Crippen draft passages are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated locators. (2) The classification rested on a 1917 grammar plus a modern verb-structure primer; the modern authorities on Tlingit prosody are Leer 1991 (dissertation) and Leer 2001 (tone paper), with Story 1966 (SIL) and Maddieson et al. 2001 (instrumental). I downloaded Leer 1991, Leer 2001, Story 1966 and Crippen's 2013 seminar notes from open archives (ANLA, tlingitlanguage.com), scanned the untexted PDFs, and read the relevant pages. sources.quote: Tone in Tlingit is phonemic, and is marked on stem vowels which have a high or low tone, thus furnishing a total of sixteen distinctive syllables. According to Velten (1939: 66): Tlingit syllables may have high, low, or indifferent pitch. The difference between high and low tone may have a semantic value ... The distinction between low and indifferent pitch, however, is less essential. Stress, though generally associated with high tone, is not phonemic. ... Minimal pairs indicate the contrastive differences in high and low tones. High tone is marked by acute accent, low by grave accent.

sources.note: Northern Tlingit has two contrastive tones, high and low, on short and long vowels, length orthogonal to tone (4 qualities x 4 = 16 vowel phonemes, plus idiolectally 'variable length' vowels in suffixes/enclitics). Some noun suffixes (possessive -i, locative-predicate -u, -tee 'all', etc.) show ALTERNATING tone - high after a low-tone stem, low after a high-tone stem - while others (e.g. -dáx̱, -náx̱) have fixed tone regardless of the stem. OT analysis: alternating tone = OCP(T) acting on TBUs lexically unspecified for tone (inserted tone obeys the OCP), fixed tone = lexically specified tone…

tone.quote: The possibilities of this objective treatment of intervals with reference to tone-language are evident. It is commonly known that in a tone-language a particular pitch level in a given voice conveys a different meaning to a sound than if that sound were intoned on another level. In a tone-language, therefore, we should expect theotetically to find two or three prominent regions for a given speaker. In this Indian voice, although there are two gross regions, we find regions within regions. A larger number of cases will be necessary before any definite conclusions can be made.

tone.quote: Tlingit dialects have various tone systems, with the majority form in Northern Tlingit having a two-way distinction between unmarked low tone and marked high tone, both of which are level. Southern Tlingit has a three- ... way tone system of low, high, and falling tones, with the falling tone having a contour that runs downward from the high tone to the low tone. Tongass Tlingit had a four-way nontonal system of syllable nuclei ... two-way tone system of Northern Tlingit may be evolving into a pitch accent system.
